chunks: "I'd start with the cheapest thing that works, which is almost always an MCU, and only move up if I can show it can't meet a requirement.
An MCU runs software, so it's the most flexible, has the fastest development, lowest cost at any volume, and mature tools.
It's limited by sequential execution: a 100 megahertz core does about 100 million simple operations per second, so it can't do something like a 64-tap FIR filter at 100 MS/s, which needs about 6.
4 billion multiply-accumulates per second. An FPGA implements the algorithm as parallel hardware.

Hundreds of DSP slices working every clock gives many billions of operations per second, deterministic nanosecond latency, and custom interfaces like a nonstandard high-speed bus or a camera sensor link.
It's reprogrammable, so low NRE and fast iteration, but the unit cost is high, power is higher than an ASIC, and the design work, RTL and timing closure, is harder.

An ASIC is custom silicon: best performance per watt and lowest unit cost at high volume, but it has huge NRE, in the millions for masks, verification and tools, 12 to 24 months of schedule, and any bug needs a costly respin.
It only makes sense at high volume, with a stable algorithm. The break-even is simple: total cost is NRE plus unit cost times volume.
With my example numbers, FPGA at 20 dollars and 150 thousand dollars NRE versus an ASIC at 1. 50 dollars and 1. 5 million NRE crosses over near 73,000 units.
Below that, FPGA; above it, consider the ASIC. In practice many products use an MCU for control and an FPGA for the fast datapath, or an SoC FPGA that has both."
